scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Suscia originated among Afro-Brazilian communities in Tocantins, with debates surrounding whether it was created by enslaved people working for gold miners or within quilombos—settlements established by escaped slaves.
The exact historic origin remains contested, and the name varies across communities as Sussa, Suça, Súcia, or Sussia.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is primarily performed during religious celebrations, particularly the monthlong festival of the Festa do Divino Espírito Santo.
Despite its sensual nature and songs centered on flirting, the local church supports and encourages the tradition as an integral piece of regional culture.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a large circle.
One male and one female dancer step into the center, hopping in circles in close proximity to one another.
Members of the outer circle clap, sing short ditties, and beat drums.
Watch for Jiquitaia Scratch, Tap-In Swap.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for Suscia relies strictly on non-electric, acoustic instrumentation.
The musical accompaniment consists of vocals, clapping, and homemade wooden drums created by hollowed-out tree trunks covered with cowhide on one end.
Listen for the Hollowed tree trunk drum with cowhide head, Acoustic string guitar, Lead and chorus vocals, Handclaps.

A high-energy acoustic texture driven by deep, handmade cowhide trunk drums and steady handclaps. Call-and-response vocals sing short, playful ditties about flirting and local humor, punctuated by acoustic guitar strumming.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Variants exist across different municipalities in Tocantins, such as Peixe, Natividade, and Arrais, primarily reflected in minor linguistic variations of the dance's name (Sussa, Suça, Súcia, Sussia).

Rooted in 18th and 19th-century Afro-Brazilian slave culture and quilombo resistance traditions in central Brazil, Suscia continues today under civic preservation programs sponsored by the state government of Tocantins.
